intro: A single word can name a thing, like perro (dog). But to tell someone what happened at a soccer game, or to ask a friend a question at a sleepover, you need a whole thought. In this unit you build whole sentences in Spanish: someone, and something they do.

You will learn the people words yo, tú, él, ella, nosotros and ellos. You will see how a verb ending like -o or -amos tells you who is acting, so Spanish speakers can often skip the word yo. You will use hablar, bailar, cantar and caminar right away.

Then you will say no, ask yes-or-no questions with a rising voice and the upside-down mark ¿, and answer in full sentences. You will also get a first taste of me gusta (I like). By the end, you can tell a short story and play a guessing game in Spanish.
bigQuestion: What does it take to say a whole thought in Spanish, and to turn it into a no or a question?

words.d: the subject — the person or thing that does the action in a sentence
the verb — the action word, like canta (sings)
I — the verb ending -o goes with yo: hablo
you (a friend) — with an accent mark; the ending is -as: hablas
we — the ending is -amos: hablamos
they — a group of boys or a mixed group; the ending is -an: hablan
to speak or talk — hablo, hablas, habla, hablamos, hablan
to walk — camino, caminas, camina, caminamos, caminan
no or not — goes right before the verb: No hablo francés
yes — always with an accent mark; si without it means if
the question — written with ¿ at the start and ? at the end
I like — me gusta bailar (I like to dance); no me gusta (I don't like)

test.q: Which form of hablar goes with tú?
test.why: For tú, drop -ar and add -as: hablas.

test.q: Which sentence means "Ana does not sing"?
test.why: No goes right before the verb, and Ana takes -a: no canta.
Él with an accent means he. El without it means the.
Spanish questions start with ¿ and end with ?.

test.q: "¿Cantas?" Which is a full no answer about you?
test.why: First no answers; second no goes before the yo form canto.

test.q: How do you say "I like to dance"?
test.why: Use the chunk me gusta, and keep the action in the -ar form.

test.q: Why can you say "Hablo inglés" without yo?
test.why: The verb ending tells who; only yo takes -o in these verbs.

test.q: A group of girls and boys dances. Which sentence fits?
test.why: A mixed group is ellos, and they take -an: bailan.
Si without an accent means if. Sí with an accent means yes.

test.q: Which is the usual Spanish order for "the big dog"?
test.why: In Spanish the describing word usually comes after the noun.

test.q: Your friend asks, "¿Te gusta el fútbol?" You don't like it. What do you say?
test.why: First no answers; no before me gusta makes it negative.

test.q: What is the stem of cantar?
test.why: Drop -ar from cantar to get the stem cant-.

test.q: The teacher asks the class, "¿Hablan inglés?" How does the class answer yes?
test.why: The class answers as nosotros, so the ending is -amos: hablamos.

write.prompt: Escribe 4–6 oraciones sobre tu día o un juego. Write 4–6 Spanish sentences about your day or a game. Use at least three different people (yo, él or ella, nosotros), one sentence with no, one yes-or-no question, and one sentence with me gusta.
tips: Use the verbs from this unit: hablar, bailar, cantar, caminar.
Put no right before the verb.
Start each question with ¿ and end it with ?.
Read your sentences aloud and let your voice rise on the question.

title: A Whole Thought in Spanish

chapters.title: Who Does What
chapters.bigQuestion: How can one small ending on a Spanish verb tell you who is doing the action?

story.title: The Game in Five Sentences
story.kicker: Sofía tells a whole soccer game with five short Spanish sentences.
paragraphs: It is Saturday morning at the park. Sofía's team, the Tigers, plays soccer against the Hawks. Her grandpa sits on the grass. He speaks Spanish, and Sofía wants to tell him the game in Spanish too. She has a small notebook and a pencil.

Sofía writes her first sentence: "Yo camino al campo" (I walk to the field). Then she writes: "Mi amigo Leo canta" (My friend Leo sings). Leo always sings before a game. Each sentence has a person and an action. That is all a sentence needs.
The game starts. Sofía writes fast: "Nosotros jugamos" (We play). The Tigers score a goal! Sofía writes: "Ellos bailan" (They dance). The whole team dances in a circle. Grandpa laughs and claps.

After the game, Sofía reads her notebook to Grandpa. For the last line she writes only "Hablo con mi abuelo" (I talk with my grandpa). She does not write yo. Grandpa smiles. "The -o at the end already says I," he tells her. "Your Spanish is smart."
story.think: Sofía left out the word yo in her last sentence. How could Grandpa still know who was talking?

lessons.title: Every Sentence Has Two Parts
lessons.mainIdea: A sentence needs someone (the subject) and something that person does (the verb).
reading: Picture Leo at the soccer game. He opens his mouth and sings. In Spanish we say "Leo canta" (Leo sings). This short sentence has two parts. Leo is the person. Canta is what he does.

The person or thing doing the action is called the *sujeto* (subject). The action word is called the *verbo* (verb). In "Ana baila" (Ana dances), Ana is the subject. Baila is the verb. A sentence needs both parts to be a whole thought.
"Leo" alone is not a sentence. It does not tell us what Leo does. "Canta" alone asks a question: who sings? Put them together and you have a whole thought: "Leo canta." Now we know who and what.

words.d: the subject — the person or thing that does the action in a sentence
the verb — the action word in a sentence, like canta (sings) or baila (dances)

look.title: Find the Two Parts
look.text: Look at three sentences from the soccer game. "Leo canta." (Leo sings.) "Ana baila." (Ana dances.) "Sofía camina." (Sofía walks.) In each one, the first word is the person. The second word is the action.
look.prompt: In "Sofía camina," which word is the subject and which word is the verb?

check.q: In the sentence "Ana baila," which word is the verb?
check.why: Baila (dances) is the action, so it is the verb. Ana is the subject, the person who dances.

check.q: Which of these is a whole sentence in Spanish?
check.why: "Leo canta" has a subject (Leo) and a verb (canta). The others are missing one of the two parts.

check.q: What does the subject of a sentence tell you?
choices: how many words are in it
check.why: The subject is the person or thing doing the action, like Leo in "Leo canta."

lessons.title: Yo, Tú, Él, Ella
lessons.mainIdea: Yo means I, tú means you (a friend), él means he and ella means she.
reading: Sometimes we use a short word instead of a name. In English we say I, you, he and she. These are called subject pronouns. A pronoun takes the place of a name. Spanish has its own set of these words.

*Yo* means I. It is not written with a capital letter unless it starts a sentence. *Tú* means you when you talk to a friend or a family member. Tú has an accent mark. Without the accent, tu means your, a different word.
*Él* means he, and *ella* means she. Él needs its accent too. Without it, el means the. So "Leo canta" can become "Él canta" (He sings). "Ana baila" can become "Ella baila" (She dances).

words.d: I — the word for yourself as the subject: yo canto (I sing)
you — for a friend, classmate or family member; always with an accent mark
he — with an accent mark; el without the accent means the
she — ella baila (she dances)

look.title: Swap the Names
look.text: Leo canta. → Él canta. (He sings.) Ana baila. → Ella baila. (She dances.) Sofía talks to Leo and says: "Tú cantas." (You sing.) Sofía talks about herself: "Yo camino." (I walk.)
look.prompt: Change "Marta canta" so it uses a pronoun instead of the name Marta.

check.q: Which word means she?
check.why: Ella means she. Él means he.

check.q: Why does tú need an accent mark?
choices: It shows the word is plural.
check.why: Tú with an accent means you. Tu without the accent means your, as in tu libro (your book).

check.q: What is the best way to say "He sings" about Leo?
check.why: He is él, with an accent. El without the accent means the, and ella means she.

lessons.title: Nosotros and Ellos
lessons.mainIdea: Nosotros means we, and ellos means they when you talk about a group.
reading: At the game, Sofía talks about her whole team. She is part of the group, so she says *nosotros* (we). "Nosotros jugamos" means we play. If the whole group is girls, she says nosotras.
Now Sofía talks about the other team. She is not part of that group. She says *ellos* (they). "Ellos corren" means they run. For a group of only girls, Spanish uses ellas.

English speakers often forget that Spanish has a boy and girl form here. Use ellos for a group of boys or a mixed group of boys and girls. Use ellas only when every person in the group is a girl or woman.

words.d: we — a group that includes you; nosotras if the whole group is girls
they — a group of boys or a mixed group; ellas for a group of only girls

look.title: A Soccer Team in Numbers
rows: jugadores en el campo por equipo (players on the field per team)
equipos en un partido (teams in a game)
minutos en un partido profesional (minutes in a pro game)
mitades en un partido (halves in a game)
look.prompt: Sofía says "nosotros" for her team. How many players on the field does that one word stand for?

check.q: Sofía talks about herself and her team. Which word does she use?
check.why: Nosotros means we, a group that includes the speaker.

check.q: A group of two boys and three girls is running. Which word means they?
check.why: Spanish uses ellos for a mixed group. Ellas is only for a group of all girls.

check.q: What does "Ellos corren" mean?
check.why: Ellos means they, so "Ellos corren" means they run.

lessons.title: Hablar Step by Step
lessons.mainIdea: To use an -ar verb, drop -ar and add an ending: -o for yo, -as for tú, -a for él or ella.
reading: Sofía wants to say she talks with Grandpa. The verb is *hablar* (to speak or to talk). This whole form, with -ar on the end, is the name of the verb. It means to talk, not who talks.

To use it, we *conjugate* the verb. That means we change the ending to match the person. First, drop -ar. That leaves habl-. Then add an ending. Yo hablo (I talk). Tú hablas (you talk). Él habla, ella habla (he talks, she talks).
A common mistake is to keep the -ar: "yo hablar." That sounds like "I to talk." Another mistake is using -o for everyone: "ella hablo." The -o ending only belongs to yo.

words.d: to speak or talk — a regular -ar verb: hablo, hablas, habla
to conjugate — to change a verb's ending so it matches who does the action

look.title: Walk Through Hablar
look.text: Start: hablar. Step 1: drop -ar → habl-. Step 2: add the ending. yo + -o → hablo. tú + -as → hablas. él + -a → habla. ella + -a → habla. Sofía says: "Yo hablo con mi abuelo." (I talk with my grandpa.)
look.prompt: Follow the same steps with cantar (to sing). What is the form for tú?

check.q: Which form goes with yo?
check.why: For yo, drop -ar and add -o: hablo.

check.q: Pick the right sentence.
check.why: For ella, drop -ar and add -a: habla. The -o ending is only for yo.

check.q: What does conjugate mean?
choices: to change the verb's ending to match who acts
to translate a word into English
check.why: To conjugate is to change the ending so the verb fits the subject: hablo, hablas, habla.

lessons.title: Endings for Groups
lessons.mainIdea: For groups, -ar verbs take -amos for nosotros and -an for ellos or ellas.
reading: Sofía's team talks in the huddle. She says "Nosotros hablamos" (We talk). The ending is *-amos*. Drop -ar from hablar, and add -amos: hablamos. Everyone in the huddle is included.
Then she looks at the other team. "Ellos hablan" (They talk). The ending is *-an*. It is just -a with an n added. That n is a little sign that means more than one person.
Now you have five endings. Yo hablo. Tú hablas. Él and ella habla. Nosotros hablamos. Ellos and ellas hablan. Say them out loud like a chant. Your ear will start to catch a wrong ending.

words.d: the -ar verb ending for nosotros (we): hablamos, cantamos, bailamos
the -ar verb ending for ellos or ellas (they): hablan, cantan, bailan

look.title: The Huddle Chant
look.text: The team claps and chants the endings. Yo hablo. Tú hablas. Ella habla. Nosotros hablamos. Ellos hablan. Clap on each ending: -o, -as, -a, -amos, -an.
look.prompt: Chant the same five forms with bailar (to dance). What is the form for nosotros?

check.q: Which form goes with nosotros?
check.why: For nosotros, drop -ar and add -amos: hablamos.

check.q: What does "Ellas hablan español" mean?
check.why: Ellas means they (all girls), and hablan is the ending for they.

check.q: Pick the right sentence.
check.why: Ellos takes the -an ending: hablan. Habla is for one person.

lessons.title: Dropping Yo
lessons.mainIdea: Spanish speakers often leave out yo, tú or nosotros because the verb ending already tells who.
reading: Look again at Sofía's last line: "Hablo con mi abuelo" (I talk with my grandpa). She did not write yo. The -o ending already says I. Only yo uses -o with these verbs, so nobody gets confused.
This is normal in Spanish. "Cantas muy bien" means you sing very well. The -as ending shows it is tú. "Bailamos" means we dance. The -amos ending shows it is nosotros.

In English you cannot drop I. "Talk with my grandpa" sounds like an order. That is why English speakers put yo in every sentence. It is not wrong, but it can sound extra strong, like saying "I myself talk."

words.d: I talk — the -o ending means yo, so the word yo can be left out
you sing — the -as ending means tú: Cantas muy bien (You sing very well)

look.title: Who Is It?
look.text: Grandpa reads three lines with no pronoun. "Camino al parque." (I walk to the park.) "Cantas muy bien." (You sing very well.) "Bailamos en el campo." (We dance on the field.) Each ending gives the answer.
look.prompt: "Hablamos con el abuelo." Which pronoun is hiding in this sentence?

check.q: In "Bailo con mi hermana," who dances?
check.why: The -o ending belongs to yo, so bailo means I dance.

check.q: Why can Spanish leave out yo in "Hablo inglés"?
check.why: The ending carries the person. Only yo uses -o in these verbs, so the meaning stays clear.

check.q: What does "Cantamos en la fiesta" mean?
check.why: The -amos ending means nosotros, so the sentence means we sing.

lessons.title: Bailar and Cantar
lessons.mainIdea: Bailar (to dance) and cantar (to sing) follow the same pattern as hablar.
reading: After the goal, the Tigers dance. Sofía writes "Ellos bailan" (They dance). The verb is *bailar* (to dance). It ends in -ar, so it works just like hablar: bailo, bailas, baila, bailamos, bailan.
Leo sings before every game. The verb is *cantar* (to sing). Drop -ar and add endings: canto, cantas, canta, cantamos, cantan. "Leo canta" means Leo sings.
These are called regular verbs. Regular means they follow the pattern with no surprises. Once you know hablar, you already know many verbs. Learn one pattern, and you can use it again and again.

words.d: to dance — regular -ar verb: bailo, bailas, baila, bailamos, bailan
to sing — regular -ar verb: canto, cantas, canta, cantamos, cantan

look.title: An Old Saying About Singing
look.text: Quien canta, su mal espanta. (Whoever sings scares away their troubles.)
look.prompt: Find the -ar verb form canta in the saying. Who is the subject: I, you or he/she?

check.q: Which form goes with tú?
check.why: For tú, drop -ar and add -as: bailas.

check.q: What does "Nosotros cantamos" mean?
check.why: Cantar means to sing, and -amos means we.

check.q: Why is cantar called a regular verb?
check.why: A regular verb follows the pattern with no surprises: canto, cantas, canta, cantamos, cantan.

lessons.title: Caminar Around the City
lessons.mainIdea: Caminar (to walk) is one more regular -ar verb you can use to tell where people go.
reading: Sofía walks to the field. She writes "Camino al campo" (I walk to the field). The verb is *caminar* (to walk). Drop -ar, add -o: camino. The -o tells us it is Sofía herself.
In Chicago, many families walk to the corner store or the park. You might hear "Caminamos al parque" (We walk to the park). Al means to the. It is a joined form of a plus el.
Here is the whole set: camino, caminas, camina, caminamos, caminan. Notice something? Every form keeps camin- at the front. Only the ending changes. The front part is called the *raíz* (stem).

words.d: to walk — regular -ar verb: camino, caminas, camina, caminamos, caminan
the stem — the part of the verb left after you drop -ar, like camin- or habl-

look.title: A Walk in the Neighborhood
look.text: Mamá: "¿Caminas a la escuela?" (Do you walk to school?) Sofía: "Sí, camino con Leo." (Yes, I walk with Leo.) Mamá: "¿Y tu abuelo?" (And your grandpa?) Sofía: "Él camina al parque." (He walks to the park.)
look.prompt: Tell Mamá that you and Leo walk to the park. Which form of caminar do you need?

check.q: What is the stem of caminar?
check.why: Drop -ar from caminar and you get the stem camin-.

check.q: Pick the right sentence for "She walks to the park."
check.why: Ella takes the -a ending: camina.

check.q: In "Caminamos al parque," what does al mean?
check.why: Al is a joined form of a (to) and el (the), so it means to the.

lessons.title: Where the Words Go
lessons.mainIdea: Spanish usually puts the subject, then the verb, then the rest, but it can move words more freely than English.
reading: Most Spanish sentences look like English ones. Subject first, then verb, then the rest. "Ana canta una canción" (Ana sings a song). "Leo camina al parque" (Leo walks to the park).

One difference is describing words. In English we say "the big dog." In Spanish the describing word usually comes after: *el perro grande* (the big dog). An English speaker might say "el grande perro." That sounds odd in Spanish.
Another difference is *no*. It goes right before the verb: "Leo no canta" (Leo does not sing). Spanish has no word for does. You will learn more about no in the next chapter.

words.d: the big dog — in Spanish the describing word usually comes after the noun
the song — Ana canta una canción (Ana sings a song)

look.title: Fix the Order
look.text: A student writes about the game: "Una rápida chica corre." The teacher helps. First the thing: una chica (a girl). Then the describing word: rápida (fast). Then the verb. "Una chica rápida corre." (A fast girl runs.)
look.prompt: Put these words in Spanish order: grande / canta / el perro. What sentence do you get?

check.q: Which is the usual Spanish way to say "the big dog"?
check.why: In Spanish the describing word usually comes after the noun: el perro grande.

check.q: Which sentence has the usual Spanish order?
check.why: Subject (Leo), then verb (camina), then the rest (al parque).

check.q: What does "Ana canta una canción" mean?
check.why: Canta means sings, and una canción means a song.

lessons.title: Telling a Game in Sentences
lessons.mainIdea: Short sentences with a subject and a conjugated verb can tell a whole story.
reading: Now you can do what Sofía did. Pick a person. Pick an action. Match the ending. "Yo camino." "Leo canta." "Nosotros hablamos." "Ellos bailan." Each one is a whole thought.
Check each sentence with three questions. Who does it? What do they do? Does the ending match the person? If ella goes with bailo, fix it: ella baila.
Spanish is spoken in 20 countries as an official language, from Mexico to Argentina to Spain. Kids in all of them build sentences this same way. Your soccer story would make sense to all of them.

words.d: the sentence — a whole thought with a subject and a verb
the game or match — el partido de fútbol (the soccer game)

look.title: Where Spanish Is Official
look.cite: Countries with Spanish as an official language (Puerto Rico, a U.S. territory, not counted)
look.prompt: Add up the rows. Do you get 20? Which part of the world has the most?

check.q: Which sentence has a mistake?
check.why: Ella needs the -a ending: ella baila. Bailo only goes with yo.

check.q: What does "El partido es hoy" tell you?
check.why: El partido means the game or match.

check.q: Which question helps you check a Spanish sentence?
choices: Does the verb ending match the person?
check.why: The ending must match the subject: hablo for yo, habla for ella, hablan for ellos.

review.q: Which form of cantar goes with ellos?

review.why: The -as ending means tú, so bailas means you dance.

review.q: Pick the right sentence for "We walk to school."

review.why: Él with an accent means he. El without an accent means the.

review.q: In the story, Sofía writes "Hablo con mi abuelo." How does Grandpa know who talks?
review.why: Only yo takes -o in these verbs, so hablo means I talk.

review.q: Which is the verb in "Mi amigo Leo canta"?
review.why: Canta (sings) is the action, so it is the verb. Mi amigo Leo is the subject.

review.q: A group of four girls sings. Which sentence fits?
review.why: A group of all girls is ellas, and they take the -an ending: cantan.

review.q: What is the first step to conjugate hablar?
review.why: First drop -ar to find the stem habl-, then add the ending for the person.

chapters.title: Saying No and Asking Yes-or-No
chapters.bigQuestion: How do you turn a Spanish sentence into a no or a yes-or-no question?

story.title: Twenty Questions at Midnight
story.kicker: At a sleepover, four friends play a guessing game using only sí and no.
paragraphs: It is Friday night at Marisol's apartment. Four friends lie in sleeping bags on the living room floor. Nobody is sleepy. Marisol's older cousin Tomás has an idea. "Let's play Twenty Questions," he says. "But in Spanish."

Tomás thinks of a famous animal. The girls can ask only yes-or-no questions. Marisol goes first. "¿Es grande?" (Is it big?) Her voice goes up at the end. Tomás answers, "Sí, es grande." (Yes, it is big.)

Ana asks, "¿Canta?" (Does it sing?) Tomás laughs. "No, no canta." (No, it does not sing.) Lucía writes each question on a notepad. She starts every question with an upside-down mark: ¿. Tomás says that is how Spanish writers warn you a question is coming.

After twelve questions, Marisol shouts, "¿Es un elefante?" (Is it an elephant?) "¡Sí!" says Tomás. Everyone cheers. Then Lucía says, "Me gusta este juego" (I like this game). Ana adds, "No me gusta dormir" (I don't like to sleep). Nobody sleeps until one o'clock.
story.think: Tomás answered "No, no canta." Why do you think he said no two times?

lessons.title: No Goes Before the Verb
lessons.mainIdea: To make a Spanish sentence negative, put no right in front of the verb.
reading: Ana's new friend asks what languages she speaks. Ana speaks English and Spanish, but not French. She says, "*No* hablo francés" (I don't speak French). She just put no in front of hablo.
Making a sentence mean not is called negation. In Spanish it takes one step. Find the verb. Put no right before it. "Leo canta" (Leo sings) becomes "Leo no canta" (Leo does not sing).

English uses extra words: do not, does not, don't. Spanish has no word for do here. A common mistake is to put no after the verb: "Leo canta no." Another is to look for a word for don't. Just use no before the verb.

words.d: no or not — goes right before the verb to make a sentence negative: No hablo francés
French (the language) — No hablo francés (I don't speak French)

look.title: One Word Changes It
look.text: Yes sentence: "Ana baila." (Ana dances.) Find the verb: baila. Put no in front. No sentence: "Ana no baila." (Ana does not dance.) Yes: "Hablamos inglés." No: "No hablamos inglés." (We don't speak English.)
look.prompt: Make this sentence negative: "Tomás canta en la fiesta."

check.q: Which sentence means "Leo does not sing"?
check.why: No goes right before the verb: Leo no canta.

check.q: What does "No hablo francés" mean?
check.why: No before hablo makes it negative, and hablo means I speak.

check.q: Where does no go in a Spanish sentence?
check.why: Spanish puts no directly in front of the verb.

lessons.title: No, No: The Double No
lessons.mainIdea: In an answer, the first no answers the question and the second no makes the verb negative.
reading: At the sleepover, Ana asks, "¿Canta?" Tomás says, "No, no canta." It looks like he said no twice by accident. He did not. Each no has its own job in the sentence.
The first no is the answer, like English no. It comes before a comma. The second no makes the verb negative, like English not. "No, no canta" means "No, it does not sing."
English speakers sometimes drop the second no and say "No, canta." That actually means "No, it sings!" The comma and the second no matter. Say both, and pause at the comma.

words.d: No, (it) doesn't… — the first no answers, the second no goes before the verb: No, no canta
the comma — separates the answer no from the rest of the sentence

look.title: Two Jobs for No
look.text: Marisol: "Tomás, ¿hablas francés?" (Tomás, do you speak French?) Tomás: "No, no hablo francés." First no = the answer. Second no = not, before the verb hablo.
look.prompt: Ana asks you, "¿Bailas?" Answer that you do not dance, using the double no.

check.q: Which answer means "No, I don't sing"?
check.why: The first no answers; the second no goes before canto to make it negative.

check.q: What does "No, canta" mean?
check.why: With only one no, before the comma, the verb canta stays positive: it sings.

check.q: In "No, no bailo," what is the job of the second no?
check.why: The second no sits before the verb bailo and means not.

lessons.title: Sí and Si
lessons.mainIdea: Sí with an accent mark means yes; si without it means if.
reading: When Tomás says yes, Lucía writes *sí* on her notepad. She puts an accent mark on the i. Without the mark, si means if. It is a different word with a different meaning.
A yes answer in a full sentence looks like this: "Sí, es grande" (Yes, it is big). Put sí first, then a comma, then the sentence. No extra word is needed.
Many heritage speakers say sí every day but forget the accent when they write. Your ear cannot hear it, but a reader can see it. Sí is yes. Si is if, as in "si llueve" (if it rains).

words.d: yes — always with an accent mark: Sí, es grande (Yes, it is big)
if — no accent mark: si llueve (if it rains)

look.title: Lucía's Notepad
look.text: Question 1: ¿Es grande? — Sí. Question 2: ¿Canta? — No. Question 3: ¿Es gris? (Is it gray?) — Sí. Question 4: ¿Vive en Chicago? (Does it live in Chicago?) — No. Every yes gets an accent mark.
look.prompt: Write Tomás's answer to "¿Es gris?" as a full sentence that starts with yes.

check.q: Which word means yes?
check.why: Sí with an accent mark means yes. Si without it means if.

check.q: What does "si llueve" mean?
check.why: Si without an accent means if.

check.q: Which is a correct yes answer to "¿Es grande?"
check.why: Yes needs the accent (sí), then a comma, then the sentence in normal order.

lessons.title: Let Your Voice Go Up
lessons.mainIdea: You can turn a Spanish sentence into a yes-or-no question by raising your voice at the end.
reading: Say "Es grande" in a flat voice. It is a statement: it is big. Now say it again, but let your voice rise at the end: "¿Es grande?" Now it asks: is it big? The words did not change.
In English we often add do or does to ask. "Do you dance?" Spanish does not need that. "Bailas" means you dance. "¿Bailas?" with a rising voice means do you dance?
This rising sound is called *la entonación* (intonation). It is the music of your voice. Listening for it helps you know if someone is telling you something or asking you something.

words.d: intonation — how your voice goes up or down; up at the end can make a question
the question — Tomás hace una pregunta (Tomás asks a question)

look.title: Same Words, New Music
look.text: Statement, flat voice: "Cantas." (You sing.) Question, voice goes up: "¿Cantas?" (Do you sing?) Statement: "Hablas inglés." (You speak English.) Question: "¿Hablas inglés?" (Do you speak English?)
look.prompt: Say "Caminas a la escuela" two ways: once as a statement and once as a question.

check.q: How can you turn "Bailas" into a question when you speak?
choices: Raise your voice at the end.
check.why: A rising voice at the end turns a statement into a yes-or-no question.

check.q: What does "¿Hablas inglés?" mean?
check.why: Hablas means you speak, and the question marks show it asks: do you speak English?

check.q: Which Spanish word do you need for do in "Do you sing?"
check.why: Spanish just uses ¿Cantas? The rising voice and question marks do the work.

lessons.title: The Upside-Down Question Mark
lessons.mainIdea: Written Spanish questions start with ¿ and end with ?, and exclamations start with ¡ and end with !.
reading: Lucía writes "¿Es grande?" The first mark is upside down: ¿. It is called the *signo de interrogación* (question mark). Spanish puts one at the start and one at the end.

Why? In a long sentence, you learn early that a question is coming. Then you can raise your voice in the right place when you read aloud. Exclamations work the same way: "¡Sí!" (Yes!) and "¡Qué bien!" (How great!)

A very common mistake is to write only the end mark: "Es grande?" That is missing a piece. Another is to put ¿ at the start of the whole line instead of where the question starts: "Tomás, ¿hablas francés?"

words.d: the question mark — Spanish uses ¿ at the start and ? at the end
the exclamation mark — Spanish uses ¡ at the start and ! at the end

look.title: Mark It Right
look.text: Wrong: Es un elefante? Right: ¿Es un elefante? Wrong: Sí! Right: ¡Sí! With a name first: Marisol, ¿bailas? (Marisol, do you dance?) The ¿ goes where the question part begins.
look.prompt: Write "Lucía, do you sing?" in Spanish with the marks in the right places.

check.q: Which question is written correctly?
check.why: Spanish questions start with ¿ and end with ?.

check.q: Which exclamation is written correctly?
check.why: Spanish exclamations start with ¡ and end with !.

check.q: Where does ¿ go in "Tomás, ¿hablas francés?"
choices: before hablas, where the question starts
check.why: The opening mark goes where the question part begins, after the name and comma.

lessons.title: Answer in a Full Sentence
lessons.mainIdea: A full answer repeats the verb with the ending for the person who answers.
reading: Your teacher asks, "¿Hablas español?" (Do you speak Spanish?) A short answer is "Sí." A full answer is "Sí, hablo español." Full answers help you practice verbs.

Watch the ending change. The question uses hablas because it is about tú. Your answer is about yo, so it uses hablo. A common mistake is to copy the question: "Sí, hablas español." That means yes, you speak Spanish.
It works for groups too. "¿Bailan ustedes?" (Do you all dance?) "Sí, bailamos." (Yes, we dance.) Ustedes means you all. The answer uses nosotros, so the ending is -amos.

words.d: the answer — una respuesta completa (a full answer)
you all — more than one person you talk to; takes the -an ending: ¿Bailan ustedes?

look.title: Flip the Ending
look.text: Question to you: ¿Cantas? → Answer about me: Sí, canto. Question to you: ¿Caminas a la escuela? → Answer: No, no camino a la escuela. Question to you all: ¿Hablan inglés? → Answer: Sí, hablamos inglés.
look.prompt: Answer "¿Bailas en las fiestas?" in a full sentence about yourself.

check.q: Your friend asks, "¿Cantas?" Which is a correct full answer about you?
check.why: The answer is about yo, so the ending changes from -as to -o: canto.

check.q: The teacher asks the class, "¿Hablan español?" Which answer fits the class?
check.why: The class answers as a group (nosotros), so the ending is -amos: hablamos.

check.q: Which is a full negative answer to "¿Caminas a la escuela?"
choices: No, no camino a la escuela.
check.why: Answer no, then no before the verb, with the yo ending: no camino.

sections.title: A First Taste of Me Gusta

lessons.title: Me Gusta: I Like
lessons.mainIdea: Me gusta plus a thing or an action means I like it: me gusta el fútbol, me gusta bailar.
reading: At the sleepover, Lucía says, "*Me gusta* este juego" (I like this game). Me gusta is how you say I like. It is a very useful phrase. It does not follow the hablo pattern, so learn it as a chunk.
Put a thing after it with el or la: "Me gusta el fútbol" (I like soccer). "Me gusta la pizza" (I like pizza). Or put an action after it, still ending in -ar: "Me gusta bailar" (I like to dance).

A common mistake is "Yo gusto el fútbol." It feels like English "I like," but in Spanish it is wrong. Stick with the chunk: me gusta. Leave the verb in its -ar form after it: me gusta cantar, not me gusta canto.

words.d: I like — me gusta el fútbol (I like soccer), me gusta bailar (I like to dance)
soccer — in most of the Spanish-speaking world, fútbol means soccer

look.title: Class Survey: What Do You Like?
look.cite: Example survey of 24 students; each student could say yes to more than one
look.prompt: Which thing do the most students like? Say it as a sentence that starts with Me gusta.

check.q: How do you say "I like to sing"?
check.why: Use the chunk me gusta, and keep the action in its -ar form: me gusta cantar.

check.q: What does "Me gusta el fútbol" mean?
check.why: Me gusta means I like, and el fútbol means soccer.

check.q: Why is "Yo gusto la pizza" a mistake?
choices: Spanish says I like with the chunk me gusta.
Pizza is not a Spanish word.
It needs no before the verb.
check.why: Spanish does not say yo gusto for I like. The correct chunk is me gusta la pizza.

lessons.title: No Me Gusta
lessons.mainIdea: To say you don't like something, put no in front: no me gusta.
reading: Ana does not want to sleep. She says, "*No me gusta* dormir" (I don't like to sleep). She put no in front of me gusta. It is the same idea as "no hablo." No goes first.
Watch the order: no, then me, then gusta. A common mistake is "Me no gusta." English speakers put not near the verb, so no ends up in the middle. In Spanish, no comes before the whole chunk.
You can answer with the double no too. "¿Te gusta el brócoli?" (Do you like broccoli?) "No, no me gusta." (No, I don't like it.) The first no answers. The second one makes it negative.

words.d: I don't like — no me gusta dormir (I don't like to sleep)
to sleep — an -ir verb; after me gusta it stays in this form

look.title: Sleepover Vote: ¿Te gusta dormir temprano?
look.cite: Example vote from the sleepover story: Do you like to go to sleep early?
look.prompt: How many friends said no? Say Ana's answer in Spanish.

check.q: Which sentence means "I don't like to dance"?
check.why: No goes in front of the whole chunk: no me gusta.

check.q: What does "No me gusta dormir" mean?
check.why: No me gusta means I don't like, and dormir means to sleep.

check.q: "¿Te gusta el brócoli?" Which answer means you do not like it?
check.why: The first no answers the question, and the second no makes me gusta negative.

lessons.title: ¿Te Gusta? Asking a Friend
lessons.mainIdea: To ask a friend if they like something, say ¿Te gusta…? and they answer with me gusta.
reading: Lucía turns to Marisol. "¿*Te gusta* el juego?" (Do you like the game?) Te gusta means you like. With a rising voice and question marks, it asks do you like?
Here is the swap to remember. The question uses te, because it is about you. The answer uses me, because it is about me. "¿Te gusta cantar?" "Sí, me gusta cantar."
A common mistake is to answer "Sí, te gusta." That means yes, you like it, which is about the other person. Switch te to me when you answer about yourself. It is like switching hablas to hablo.

words.d: you like (to a friend) — ¿Te gusta bailar? (Do you like to dance?)
the game — Me gusta este juego (I like this game)

look.title: Sleeping Bag Talk
look.text: Lucía: "¿Te gusta el juego?" (Do you like the game?) Marisol: "¡Sí, me gusta!" (Yes, I like it!) Lucía: "¿Te gusta dormir?" (Do you like to sleep?) Marisol: "No, no me gusta." (No, I don't like it.)
look.prompt: Ask a partner if they like to sing. Then answer their question about you.

check.q: How do you ask a friend "Do you like to dance?"
check.why: Te gusta means you like; keep bailar in the -ar form, and use ¿ and ?.

check.q: Your friend asks, "¿Te gusta la pizza?" You like it. What do you say?
check.why: Switch te to me when you answer about yourself: Sí, me gusta.

check.q: What does "¿Te gusta el juego?" mean?
check.why: Te gusta means you like, and the question marks make it ask.

lessons.title: Playing Twenty Questions
lessons.mainIdea: With sí, no, rising questions and me gusta, you can play a whole guessing game in Spanish.
reading: Now you have all the tools from the sleepover. You can ask with a rising voice and ¿ ?. You can answer sí or no. You can say no before a verb. You can talk about what you like.
Try the game. One person thinks of an animal. Others ask: "¿Es grande?" "¿Es pequeño?" (Is it small?) "¿Canta?" The answers must be full: "Sí, es pequeño." "No, no canta."
Keep count on your fingers. Twenty questions is the limit. When you are ready, guess with a question: "¿Es un gato?" (Is it a cat?) End with "¡Me gusta este juego!" if you had fun.

words.d: small or little — ¿Es pequeño? (Is it small?); pequeña for a feminine noun
big — the same form for masculine and feminine: el elefante grande, la casa grande

look.title: A Round of the Game
look.text: Ana thinks of an animal. Lucía: "¿Es grande?" Ana: "No, no es grande." Marisol: "¿Es pequeño?" Ana: "Sí, es pequeño." Tomás: "¿Canta?" Ana: "Sí, canta." Lucía: "¿Es un pájaro?" (Is it a bird?) Ana: "¡Sí!"
look.prompt: Think of an animal. Write three yes-or-no questions a friend could ask to guess it.

check.q: In the round, Ana answers "No, no es grande." What does she mean?
check.why: The first no answers; no before es makes it negative: it is not big.

check.q: Which is a correctly written guess?
check.why: The question starts with ¿ and ends with ?, around the whole question.

check.q: The animal is small and sings. Which question gets a sí?
check.why: The animal sings, so the answer to ¿Canta? is Sí, canta.

review.q: Which sentence means "We don't speak French"?
review.why: No goes right before the verb, and nosotros takes -amos: no hablamos.
Sí with an accent means yes. Si without it means if.

review.q: "¿Bailas?" Which is a full yes answer about you?
review.why: The question uses tú (bailas); your answer is about yo, so it is bailo.
Spanish questions begin with ¿ and end with ?.

review.q: In the story, why did Tomás say "No, no canta"?
choices: The first no answers and the second means not.
Spanish always says every word twice.
review.why: Each no has a job: the answer, then not before the verb canta.

review.q: How do you say "I don't like soccer"?
review.why: Put no in front of the chunk me gusta: no me gusta el fútbol.

review.q: How can you make "Cantas" a question when you speak?
choices: Raise your voice at the end.
review.why: A rising voice at the end turns a statement into a yes-or-no question.
Te gusta means you like, and the question marks make it a question.
